Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The first third of the story relies effectively on summary and exposition to compress roughly a decade of history, establishing the narrator's college friendship with Q, Q's seemingly effortless competence, and their gradual drifting apart after graduation. This background information is essential for building the narrator's psychological investment in Q—specifically, the narrator's desire to see Q fail or reveal a flaw. 

Once the narrator spots Q at the town pool, the story shifts into a detailed, real-time scene. Through the overheard dialogue between Q and Lydia, and subsequently between Q and his daughter, the plot unfolds dramatically. The reader witnesses Q's flaw firsthand (his inability to hold firm on bad news out of a mix of kindness and self-serving convenience) rather than just being told about it. The initial exposition makes the tension of the pool scene meaningful, creating a well-paced and engaging narrative.
